method: Re-verified the three earlier notes (ALICE_SCRIPT_FACTCHECK.md, MEGASPEED_DETAILS_FACTCHECK.md, RESEARCH_V2.md) with ~35 fresh WebSearch queries on 2026-11-18, prioritising original/official outlets (NVIDIA IR/GlobeNewswire, SEC 8-K, CBS, NPR, Malaysiakini, Bernama, SCMP, Reuters/NYT syndications). Findings rest on search-result summaries; no article body was read in full. Cross-checked against the approved script (alice/SCRIPT.md v1/v3/v4).
access_limits: WebFetch failed with DNS/allowlist errors for every host tried: nvidianews.nvidia.com, www.sec.gov, finance.yahoo.com, www.scmp.com, kutv.com, fortune.com (and earlier cnbc.com, cbsnews.com, thenextweb.com, tweaktown.com, npr.org). Not attempted: bloomberg.com, nytimes.com, wsj.com, ft.com, reuters.com (paywalled/previously refused). No primary Bloomberg, NYT, FT, WSJ or Reuters text, Federal Register entry, BIS release, MHA statement or MFA transcript was read. These hosts must be allowed in the session's network settings to read primaries.

claims.claim: Alice Huang (also reported as Huang Le) is the businesswoman at the centre of the story; private individual; any public statement.
claims.safe_wording: Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. She has made no public statement.
claims.evidence: Multiple outlets citing NYT report her name is also given as Huang Le and that she is not related to Jensen Huang. C4ADS (via press) says shares of Megaspeed were transferred in March 2023 to Huang Le Limited, a BVI company. Reported as a Chinese citizen. NYT-derived coverage says she did not respond to the Times; no statement from her found in any search.

claims.cautions: Treat as a private individual: no public office, no public statements. Do not speculate about her whereabouts or personal life; no 'honey trap'/'mistress'/sexualised framing in title, thumbnail or VO. Nationality 'Chinese citizen' rests on press reports only.

claims.claim: Her role at Megaspeed: founder? CEO/chair? Took control 2023? Left Aug 30, 2025?
claims.safe_wording: "Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive" (or "widely reported as Megaspeed's former CEO"). Megaspeed says she left on August 30, 2025.
claims.evidence: Megaspeed's emailed statement (Nov 15, 2026, via AP/Reuters/AFP) says she left effective Aug 30, 2025 and has no role. Singapore corporate records (via press) show her as a director, reportedly also managing director, from March to November 2023; C4ADS says she became controlling shareholder in March 2023 via Huang Le Limited, which sold/transferred the company in Nov 2023 (to Swiftdata, owned by Tan Yong Pong, now Megaspeed's director/CEO; accounts differ on the buyer). Megaspeed has rejected suggestions she served as its chief executive (SCMP headline/summary), though many outlets (incl. CBS) still call her former CEO. Culper Research (short seller) cited an employee saying she stayed involved in daily operations. 'Founder' is not supported consistently.

claims.cautions: Do NOT say 'founder'. Do NOT state 'She was CEO' or 'who ran Megaspeed' as fact: the title is disputed by the company and the records show director/MD Mar-Nov 2023. 'Took control in 2023' is OK only as 'became controlling shareholder in 2023, per C4ADS'. SCMP page could not be opened (blocked); wording from search summary.

claims.claim: Megaspeed is a Singapore cloud company, founded 2023, that buys NVIDIA servers and rents compute.
claims.safe_wording: Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud company that buys NVIDIA-powered servers and rents out the computing power.
claims.evidence: Described across coverage as a Singapore-based cloud computing company and NVIDIA customer/cloud partner that buys equipment with NVIDIA processors and makes the capacity available to customers. Generally described as a 2023 spinoff of Chinese gaming/cloud firm 7Road; filings cited by press indicate the entity dates to 2015 as 7Road International and was renamed Megaspeed International in March 2023. Data centres in Malaysia and Indonesia.

claims.claim: Bloomberg: at least $4.6B of NVIDIA hardware imported (Malaysian/Indonesian customs, 2023-Nov 2025, ~136,000 GPUs).
claims.safe_wording: "Bloomberg's analysis of customs records puts Megaspeed's NVIDIA hardware imports at about $4.6 billion." (Prefer 'imported' over 'bought'.)
claims.evidence: Search summaries of Bloomberg's investigation (dated ~Dec 22, 2025 per secondaries) say Megaspeed and affiliates imported about $4.6B of hardware with roughly 136,000 GPUs since its 2023 founding, per Malaysian and Indonesian customs data compiled by Big Trade Data. Bloomberg follow-up (Nov 2026, via TheNextWeb headline) found ~17,544 GB300 (~$787M) imported in Nov 2025 after NVIDIA said it cut Megaspeed off. Other figures (NYT ~$2B and >=$4.8B Speedmatrix Jun 2024-Feb 2026; WSJ ~$12B orders; The Information ~$7.5B) are not comparable.

claims.cautions: Bloomberg original not opened (paywall/blocked); Dec 22, 2025 date from secondaries only. Imports are not proof of diversion. Do not attribute the $4.6B to 2022-2025/C4ADS. 'At least' vs 'about' differs by secondary: 'about' is safer.

claims.claim: Speedmatrix is Megaspeed's Malaysian affiliate/subsidiary, importer and data-centre operator.
claims.safe_wording: Speedmatrix, Megaspeed's Malaysian affiliate, which imported the hardware and runs its data centres there.
claims.evidence: Malaysia's MITI (Nov 13, 2026) said it never cleared Megaspeed or its Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix and leads a probe with Customs into whether chips imported by Speedmatrix were re-exported in breach of the Strategic Trade Act 2010. Police say they have probed alleged diversion since April 2025. US officials (via NYT) say servers went to Speedmatrix-run facilities in Malaysia and Indonesia. FT (via press) says Alibaba's Apex lent to Speedmatrix in June 2024.

claims.claim: Alibaba is the anchor/largest customer renting Megaspeed compute in SE Asia.
claims.safe_wording: "Reports say its biggest client is Alibaba." Better: "The Financial Times reports its largest client is Alibaba."
claims.evidence: Bloomberg (Dec 2025, documents reviewed) reported Megaspeed rents NVIDIA chips to Alibaba at several SE Asian sites. FT (Nov 2026, two people familiar, via secondaries) said Alibaba was the anchor customer from the outset and remains the largest client, and that Alibaba's Singapore unit Apex lent to Speedmatrix in June 2024. No Alibaba response found; Alibaba is not reported as a target of any probe.

claims.claim: US export controls: Oct 7, 2022 rule; Oct 17, 2023 update; scope; not all NVIDIA products banned; Nov 16, 2026 remote-access rule.
claims.safe_wording: "U.S. rules require a license to ship NVIDIA's most advanced AI chips to China." (Not 'block all sales'.) "On November 16, Commerce issued a rule to close the remote-access gap."
claims.evidence: BIS issued controls Oct 7, 2022; the Oct 17, 2023 package (interim final rules + Entity List rule; most provisions effective Nov 17, 2023) tightened thresholds and extended licence requirements to firms headquartered in China/Macau/arms-embargoed countries. Lower-performance or compliant parts have been sold (e.g., H20; Jan 15, 2026 BIS rule revised review policy for certain advanced chips to China). Nov 16, 2026: BIS interim final rule requiring licences to supply chips to data centres providing significant compute to companies headquartered in Macau/Country Group D:5, plus licences for advanced chip exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand; reported exemption for US-run data centres.

claims.claim: Before Nov 2026, Chinese firms renting compute in overseas data centres was legal (cloud loophole).
claims.safe_wording: "Renting that computing power to Chinese firms from data centres abroad was generally allowed, until a new U.S. rule this month. Shipping the top chips into China needed a license."
claims.evidence: Coverage (Bloomberg via secondaries, CNN Nov 14, Sovereign Magazine) says renting AI chip capacity to Chinese firms for use outside China was generally permitted under US rules; the Nov 16, 2026 BIS rule was explicitly framed as closing that 'loophole'. Caveat: the Oct 2023 rule already required licences for exports to China-headquartered firms' overseas entities, and the Jan 2026 rule anticipated cloud providers screening restricted parties.

claims.cautions: Use 'generally allowed' / 'wasn't banned', past tense, and mention it has now been restricted. Legality of any specific Megaspeed transaction is under investigation; don't say Megaspeed's business was 'legal' as a blanket fact.

claims.claim: Physical diversion to China established? Probes (US Commerce, DOJ, Singapore, Malaysia); charges; Singapore findings on Alice.
claims.safe_wording: "Investigators in the U.S., Singapore and Malaysia are probing whether chips reached China. Nothing has been proven, and no charges have been filed."
claims.evidence: No diversion established. Commerce probe (from 2024) was paused/transferred and is now a DOJ criminal inquiry (NYT via press); DOJ also reportedly probing Super Micro smuggling by Huang-linked entities (Bloomberg). AG Todd Blanche (Nov 12) said DOJ had not concluded she was a spy. Singapore MHA (Nov 12, 2026): police found insufficient evidence she committed offences linked to Megaspeed's possible false declarations; stern warning; re-entry ban for knowingly giving inaccurate information about her role; she left Singapore Feb 26, 2026; not investigated for espionage; probe into Megaspeed and six others ongoing. Malaysia MITI/police probing; no re-export established. NVIDIA says it found no evidence of diversion.

blocking_issues: C02: Script states 'She was CEO of Megaspeed' (v1) / 'former CEO' (v3) / 'who ran' (v4) as fact. Megaspeed rejects that she was its chief executive; records show director/managing director Mar-Nov 2023. Replace with 'a former Megaspeed executive' (or 'widely reported as its former CEO').

C07: v1 line 'U.S. rules block sales of these chips to China' overstates; use 'U.S. rules restrict' or 'require a license to ship NVIDIA's top AI chips to China'. v3/v4 'Shipping chips into China was [banned]' -> 'Shipping the top chips into China needed a license.'
C04: v4 changed 'imported' to 'bought'; Bloomberg's figure is customs import data for Megaspeed and affiliates. Keep 'imported' and 'about $4.6 billion' (attributed to Bloomberg).
C11/C01: Opening line 'a woman U.S. officials suspect of spying for China' should be attributed ('reportedly' / 'according to The New York Times') since it precedes the NYT attribution.
non_blocking_notes: C15: 'routine business' is a paraphrase (Reuters did not quote verbatim); OK as spoken paraphrase, never in on-screen quotes. 'standard business with a customer' is closer.
C06: 'largest client: Alibaba' must stay attributed ('reports say'/'the FT reports'); FT text not read.
C08: say 'wasn't banned' in past tense and ideally note the Nov 16 rule now restricts it.
C12/C09: re-check 'no charges' and Huang's status (reinstatement chatter unverified) on upload day.
C13: board statement dates from Nov 8, before the resignation; past tense 'said'.
